issues: Whether a person continuously absent from Canada for approximately sixteen years for full-time religious training, while maintaining residential ties (furnished apartment, financial accounts, provincial health coverage, social and civic ties, sole Canadian passport, no foreign tax filings), remains a factual resident of Canada for income tax purposes.
The weight of secondary residential ties and the intention to return in determining Canadian tax residency during a prolonged absence for full-time studies.

Whether the purpose of the absence (full-time training available only overseas) and the fixed end-date (completion of the program) distinguish the situation from a permanent departure or severance of residential ties.
The onus of proof on the question of Canadian tax residency when the issue is raised for the first time at the hearing stage rather than at the objection stage.

Whether the Crown is precluded from raising a residency argument at the hearing stage when its own pleaded assumption was that the taxpayer was resident and the argument was never raised at the objection stage.

Whether a prior written confirmation by the revenue agency that the taxpayer remained a factual resident while studying creates a legitimate expectation or estoppel that prevents the agency from taking a contrary position.

The residency and primary caregiver eligibility requirements for the Canada Child Benefit or its predecessor benefit, and the validity of a primary caregiver designation where the spouse has never resided in Canada.
key_facts: Continuous absence from Canada for approximately sixteen years solely to complete a full-time religious training program available only overseas.

Maintenance of a furnished apartment in parents' Canadian home, Canadian bank and investment accounts, a registered education plan, provincial health coverage, synagogue and mentor relationships, party membership and voting, and a sole Canadian passport.
No foreign tax return ever filed; no change in circumstances at any identifiable point after departure.
Standing offer of a teaching post in Canada upon completion of the program.
Revenue agency previously confirmed in writing that the taxpayer remained a factual resident while studying.
Crown's initial ground for clawback (invalid primary caregiver designation) was abandoned at the hearing; the residency argument was raised for the first time at that stage.
Crown's own pleaded assumption at the objection stage was that the taxpayer was resident.
causes_of_action: Objection to reassessment (clawback of child benefits) before the Tax Court of Canada
